title: How would you estimate how many parcels are delivered to UK homes each year?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many parcels are delivered to UK homes each year?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: Roughly 2.6 billion parcels a year are delivered to UK homes: about 28M households receiving an average of 1.8 parcels a week, over 52 weeks. That weekly average is the number that matters, so build it from a few types of household rather than guessing it. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many parcels are delivered to UK homes each year?

Agree the scope before you start. The question says "homes", so deliveries to offices and shops are out. Decide on three grey areas and say what you chose:

  • Grocery deliveries: a supermarket van with eight crates is one delivery, not a parcel. Leave it out.
  • Lockers and pick-up points: the parcel is still bought by a household. Include it.
  • Returns: these travel from homes, not to them. Leave them out.
"I'll count parcels addressed to UK households, including those sent to lockers, and exclude grocery deliveries, returns and anything sent to businesses."

The approach: households × parcels per week × weeks

Start from households, not people. Parcels are delivered to an address, and a family of four sharing one door does not get four times as many parcels as a single person. Then multiply by parcels per household per week and by 52.

The weekly rate drives everything, and one average is hard to defend. So split households into groups that behave differently. This is the same weighted average technique you would use in any segmented estimate.

Step by step

Start with 28M UK households (the ONS counted about 28.6M in 2024).

SegmentShare of homesParcels a weekContribution
Heavy online shoppers (families, frequent buyers)30%41.2
Regular shoppers50%10.5
Light or rare shoppers (many older households)20%0.50.1
Weighted average100%1.8
  1. 28M households × 1.8 parcels a week = 50.4M parcels a week.
  2. × 52 weeks = about 2.6B parcels a year.

The heavy group is 30% of homes but two thirds of the parcels (1.2 of 1.8). That is the group a carrier or retailer would want to understand first.

Sanity check from a second angle

Per person. 2.6B ÷ 68M people is about 38 parcels a person a year, or roughly three a month. That feels right for a country where online shopping is routine.

From the supply side. Assume a delivery driver drops about 120 parcels a day and works 300 days a year, so 36,000 parcels a year. Then 2.6B parcels need about 72,000 full-time drivers. Tens of thousands of drivers across several carriers fits what you see on any residential street: a handful of different vans most days. If the maths had needed a million drivers, you would know the weekly rate was too high.

Against the published total. Ofcom's post monitoring report counted about 3.9B parcels in the UK in 2023-24, covering every sender and recipient, including businesses and returns. Our 2.6B to homes is about two thirds of that, which is plausible: most parcels go to consumers, but not all.

Which assumption matters most?

The heavy segment. If it is 20% of homes rather than 30% (and the regular group grows to 60%), the weekly average drops to 0.8 + 0.6 + 0.1 = 1.5 and the total to about 2.2B. Using a flat two parcels a week for every home would instead give 2.9B. Say which way you lean and why.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I get about 2.6 billion parcels a year to homes, from 28 million households at 1.8 a week. Two thirds of that comes from the 30% of homes that shop online heavily, so that's where I'd want real data. As a check, it's about three parcels per person a month and needs around 70,000 drivers, which both feel right."

A weak answer multiplies 68M people by "a couple of parcels a week" and gets about 7B, more than the total Ofcom measured for the whole market. Starting from people instead of homes is what breaks it.

Common mistakes

  • Using people instead of households. This inflates the answer by the household size, roughly 2.4x.
  • Ignoring the scope. Business deliveries, groceries and returns can each move the answer by hundreds of millions. Name them at the start.
  • Forgetting seasonality when it matters. A yearly total is fine for market size, but a carrier planning capacity cares about the weeks before Christmas, when volumes run well above average.
  • Stopping at volume. If the client is a carrier, revenue depends on price per parcel and on how many deliveries succeed first time.

Practise it

1. A carrier earns an average of $3.50 per home delivery. What is the revenue pool for home parcels?

Show the answer

2.6B × $3.50 = about $9.1B a year. Using the unrounded 2.62B gives $9.2B; either is fine if you say you rounded.

2. In the busiest weeks before Christmas, volumes run at 1.5 times the average. How many parcels a week is that, and how many extra drivers are needed?

Show the answer

Average week: 50.4M. Peak week: 50.4M × 1.5 = about 76M parcels. That is 50% more work, so roughly 50% more driver capacity: about 36,000 extra on top of 72,000, through temporary hires, longer shifts or more parcels per drop.

3. One in ten parcels to the heavy segment is returned. How many returns does that create a year?

Show the answer

Heavy segment parcels: 28M × 30% × 4 × 52 = about 1.75B a year. 10% of that is about 175M returns. Returns are a separate flow from homes to retailers, which is why we left them out of the main answer.

Where to practise next

For another household-based estimate, try delivery pizzas in the UK. To see how carriers make money from this volume, read how online retailers make money. The full method is in how to answer a market sizing question, and you can drill timed prompts in the market sizing drills.
